First, $\mathcal{AG}(1,1,1)$ is not connected as it has two connected components - $\{123,231,312\}$ and $\{132,321,213\}.$ Now, we need to show that if $x_{i}\geq\frac{1}{2}(x_{1}+x_{2}+x_{3})$ holds for some $i,$ the anagraph is also disconnected. Without loss of generality, let this be the case for $i=1.$ If $x_{1}>\frac{1}{2}(x_{1}+x_{2}+x_{3}),$ then the anagraph has at least one vertex, but all of its vertices are isolated by Observation 2.2.1, so the graph is disconnected. If $x_{1}=\frac{1}{2}(x_{1}+x_{2}+x_{3}),$ consider the canonical word $\chi.$ It is clearly only connected to words whose last $x_{1}$ letters equal $1.$ However, any word whose last $x_{1}$ letters equal 1 is only connected to words whose first $x_{1}$ letters equal 1. In particular, this means that for any word $\omega$ in the connected component of $\chi,$ either its first $x_{1}$ letters or its last $x_{1}$ letters are all $1$ ’s. Thus, the anagraph is disconnected in this case as well.

Case 4. $n\geq 4.$ First, if there exists some $i$ such that $x_{i}\geq\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{n}x_{j},$ the anagraph is disconnected. This follows in the same way as in the case $n=3.$ If, on the other hand, $x_{i}<\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{n}x_{j}$ holds for all $i,$ we need to show that the anagraph is connected. We do so by repeatedly reducing the alphabet size as follows. Let $(y^{(n)}_{1},y^{(n)}_{2},\ldots,y^{(n)}_{n})=(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n}).$ While $k>4,$ find $u,v$ such that $y^{(k)}_{u}$ and $y^{(k)}_{v}$ are the smallest two (tiebreaks handled arbitrarily) numbers in $(y^{(k)}_{1},y^{(k)}_{2},\ldots,y^{(k)}_{k}).$ Then, define $(y^{(k-1)}_{1},\ldots,y^{(k-1)}_{k-1})=red_{u,v}(y^{(k)}_{1},y^{(k)}_{2},\ldots,y^{(k)}_{k}).$ Note that in doing this operation, the sum $\sum_{j=1}^{k}y^{(k)}_{j}$ remains unchanged. This shows that the condition $y^{(k)}_{i}<\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{k}y^{(k)}_{j}$ holds for all $i$ and $k\geq 4.$ Indeed, the only number that appears in $(y^{(k)}_{1},\ldots,y^{(k)}_{k}),$ but not in $(y^{(k+1)}_{1},y^{(k+1)}_{2},\ldots,y^{(k+1)}_{k+1}),$ is $y^{(k+1)}_{u}+y^{(k+1)}_{u}.$ As $k\geq 4,$ the choice of $u,v,$ guarantees that $y^{(k+1)}_{u}+y^{(k+1)}_{v}\leq\frac{2}{5}\sum_{j=1}^{k}y^{(k)}_{j}<\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{k}y^{(k)}_{j}.$

After performing this operation, we are left with four numbers $y^{(4)}_{1},y^{(4)}_{2},y^{(4)}_{3},y^{(4)}_{4}.$ Write them in decreasing order as $y_{1}\geq y_{2}\geq y_{3}\geq y_{4}.$ We know that $y_{1}\leq\frac{1}{2}(y_{1}+y_{2}+y_{3}+y_{4}).$ We now consider two cases for these numbers.

Case 4.1. If $y_{1}=y_{2}=y_{3}=y_{4},$ then $\mathcal{AG}(y_{1},y_{2},y_{3},y_{4})$ is connected by Lemma 5.2.2. From Proposition 5.1.1, so is $\mathcal{AG}(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n}).$

Case 4.2. If the four numbers are not equal, this means that $y_{3}+y_{4}<y_{1}+y_{2}.$ Therefore, $\mathcal{AG}(y_{1},y_{2},y_{3}+y_{4})$ is connected by Lemma 5.2.3. From Proposition 5.1.1, so is $\mathcal{AG}(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n}).$ ∎

#### Remark 5.2.4.

We end with a remark about a further global property of the anagraphs, beyond the ones listed in Definition 1.2.3. Combining together our result for the parity of the degrees in an anagraph - Corollary 3.3.6 - and our result for the connectivity of anagraphs - Theorem 5.2.1 - we derive a necessary and sufficient condition for an anagraph to be Eulerian.

## 6 Further Directions

As the non-asymptotic study of anagrams without fixed letters is a rather new field, we end with a multitude of directions for further work. Of course, we are most interested in fully resolving Problem 1.3.1, Problem 1.3.4, and Problem 1.3.11. Here, we make a few remarks about these problems.

Arithmetic Questions: We are especially interested in improving the running-time of Corollary 3.3.3, so that larger primes can also be handled efficiently. As discussed in Remark 3.3.5, this direction of study can be very useful in computing ${\mathsf{A}}().$ Similarly, one could think of extending the result to prime-powers.

Ordinal Questions: Since our result about Schur-Concavity makes very substantial progress in the case of $\sum_{i}x_{i}=\sum_{j}y_{j},$ we believe that the setting of equal sums is more tractable. Beyond that, we are interested in improving the constant $\frac{1}{2}$ in Theorem 4.3.4. Namely, we make the following conjecture.

#### Conjecture 6.0.1.

Suppose that $x_{i}<\max(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n}).$ Then,

$$ {\mathsf{A}}(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{i-1},x_{i},x_{i+1},\ldots,x_{n})\leq{\mathsf{A}}(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{i-1},x_{i}+1,x_{i+1},\ldots,x_{n}). $$

Questions on Anagraphs: In light of the strong connection between hamiltonicity and vertex-transitivity [6], we make the following conjecture.

#### Conjecture 6.0.2.

All, but finitely many, connected anagraphs are hamiltonian.

We exclude finitely many anagraphs to avoid $\mathcal{AG}(1,1)$ (which is a single edge) and the four known connected vertex-transitive graphs which are not hamiltonian [12]. Note that if this conjecture is true, one potentially only needs to prove it for anagraphs over alphabet of size four. This follows from Proposition 5.1.1 and the method used in the proof of Theorem 5.2.1.

&g(\xi_{1},\lambda_{\ell}),g(\xi_{2},\lambda_{\ell}),\ldots,g(\xi_{k},\lambda_{\ell})\end{split} $$

Case 2) If $s(\chi_{1})=s(\chi_{2}).$ Without loss of generality, we can index $\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\ldots,\lambda_{\ell}$ such that $s(\chi_{1})=\lambda_{1}.$ Then, the following is a hamilton path connecting the two vertices:

$$ \begin{split}&g(\zeta_{1},\lambda_{1}),g(\zeta_{2},\lambda_{2}),g(\zeta_{3},\lambda_{2}),\ldots,g(\zeta_{k},\lambda_{2}),\\
&g(\zeta_{1},\lambda_{2}),g(\zeta_{2},\lambda_{3}),g(\zeta_{3},\lambda_{3}),\ldots,g(\zeta_{k},\lambda_{3}),\\
&\vdots\\
&g(\zeta_{1},\lambda_{\ell-1}),g(\zeta_{2},\lambda_{\ell}),g(\zeta_{3},\lambda_{\ell}),\ldots,g(\zeta_{k},\lambda_{\ell}),\\
&g(\xi_{1},\lambda_{\ell}),g(\xi_{2},\lambda_{1}),g(\xi_{3},\lambda_{1}),\ldots,g(\xi_{k},\lambda_{1}).\end{split} $$

4) Pancyclicity. Suppose that $\mathcal{AG}(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n-2},x_{n-1}+x_{n})$ is pancyclic. In particular, this means that it is hamiltonian. Furthermore, as the graph is vertex-transitive, it is also vertex-pancyclic, which means that for any $\omega$ in its vertex set and number $3\leq k\leq|V(\mathcal{AG}(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n-2},x_{n-1}+x_{n}))|,$ there exists a simple cycle of length $k$ containing the vertex $\omega.$

We want to show that $\mathcal{AG}(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n-2},x_{n-1},x_{n})$ is also pancyclic. Take any $k$ such that

$$ \begin{split}3\leq k\leq\;&\\
\leq\;&|V(\mathcal{AG}(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n}))|\\
=\;&\binom{x_{1}+x_{2}+\cdots+x_{n}}{x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n-2},x_{n-1},x_{n}}\\
=\;&\binom{x_{1}+x_{2}+\cdots+x_{n}}{x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n-2},x_{n-1}+x_{n}}\binom{x_{n-1}+x_{n}}{x_{n}}\\
=\;&|V(\mathcal{AG}(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n-2},x_{n-1}+x_{n}))|\binom{x_{n-1}+x_{n}}{x_{n}}.\end{split} $$

We need to show that there exists a cycle in $\mathcal{AG}(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n})$ of size $k.$ We assume that $k<|V(\mathcal{AG}(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n}))|$ as we have already shown that the reduction preserves hamiltonicity. Denote $s=|V(\mathcal{AG}(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n-2},x_{n-1}+x_{n}))|.$ Suppose that $k=ms+r,$ where $r$ is the residue upon division by $s$ and $m<\binom{x_{n-1}+x_{n}}{x_{n}}$ is the quotient. Since $s\geq 5$ (one can trivially check that there does not exist a pancyclic anagraph on less than 5 vertices with Theorem 5.2.1), we can clearly write $k$ as a sum of $t\in\{m,m+1\}$ numbers $s_{1},s_{2},\ldots,s_{t},$ such that $3\leq s_{i}\leq s$ for all $i\in[t].$ Since $t\leq\binom{x_{n-1}+x_{n}}{x_{n}},$ we can also choose $t$ different words $\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\ldots,\lambda_{t},$ each composed of exactly $x_{n-1}$ letters $n-1$ and $x_{n}$ letters $n.$ Furthermore, for each $i\in[t],$ there exists a cycle $\xi_{i,1},\xi_{i,2},\ldots,\xi_{i,s_{i}}$ such that $\xi_{i,s_{i}}=\xi_{i+1,1}$ when $i<t$ also holds. This follows from the fact that the reduced anagraph is vertex-pancyclic. Thus,

$$ \begin{split}&g(\xi_{1,1},\lambda_{1}),g(\xi_{1,2},\lambda_{1}),\ldots,g(\xi_{1,s_{1}},\lambda_{1}),\\
&g(\xi_{2,1},\lambda_{2}),g(\xi_{2,2},\lambda_{2}),\ldots,g(\xi_{2,s_{2}},\lambda_{2}),\\
\vdots\\
&g(\xi_{t,1},\lambda_{t}),g(\xi_{t,2},\lambda_{t}),\ldots,g(\xi_{t,s_{t}},\lambda_{t})\\
\end{split} $$

is a simple cycle of length $k$ in $\mathcal{AG}(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n}).$

5) Edge-Pancyclicity. Edge pancyclicity follows in absolutely the same way as pancyclicity, except that we choose the first cycle $\xi_{1,1},\xi_{1,2},\ldots,\xi_{1,s_{1}}$ so that $(\xi_{1,1},\xi_{1,2})$ corresponds to the desired edge $(\chi_{1},\chi_{2})$ of $\mathcal{AG}(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n})$ to be included. We distinguish two cases $s(\chi_{1})=s(\chi_{2})$ and $s(\chi_{1})\neq s(\chi_{2})$ and handle them in absolutely the same way as for hamilton-connectivity. ∎
